newsitem.title: INDIA: Fledgling Indian government faces first major test.
newsitem.headline: Fledgling Indian government faces first major test.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's week-old government on Tuesday moved to overcome its first potential crisis after the leader of his party refused to step down in a $280 million corruption case.
Leaders of Gujral's Janata Dal party said senior party officials were expected to meet soon to try to absorb the shock waves from the "animal fodder" scandal.

Janata Dal chief Laloo Prasad Yadav on Monday defiantly rejected calls from left-wing parties in the governing United Front coalition to quit as chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar in a scandal over animal fodder.

"Why should I resign?" Yadav told reporters late on Monday after the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said it would prosecute him and 55 others in the decade-old case. "I will go to the people's court for its verdict."
The Janata Dal is the biggest component in Gujral's 15-party United Front alliance with 45 of the coalition's 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house of parliament.
The 10 billion rupee ($280 million) scandal, stretching back more than a decade but uncovered last year, involved the alleged misuse of funds for an animal welfare scheme.

Janata Dal leaders acknowledged that Yadav's refusal to resign created problems for Gujral's government, which took office on April 21 after his predecessor, former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, was toppled in a confidence vote in parliament.
"Naturally this poses a problem for us," a senior Janata Dal leader who asked not to be identified told Reuters.
"If he refuses to step down, it will make it difficult for us to run parliament and maintain public opinion."
Asked if the prosecution of Yadav was a setback for the Janata Dal, Railways Minister Ram Vilas Paswan said: "It definitely affects us."
Paswan said Janata Dal leaders would meet soon in the capital to decide on Yadav's leadership role. "It will be a collective decision of the party," Paswan said.
Yadav, who says he is innocent, shrugged off a call by the four leftwing parties in Gujral's 15-party coalition to quit.
"He is a defiant kind of character. I don't think he wants to conform to the norms," the senior Janata Dal leader said.
Yadav's refusal to quit as Bihar chief minister put pressure on Gujral's government to consider recommending to President Shankar Dayal Sharma that he force Yadav to resign.
"The (federal) government will be under pressure to dismiss the state government," the senior Janata Dal leader said.
Gujral was also under pressure to consider asking junior Rural Areas and Employment Minister Chandradeo Prasad Varma to quit since he was one of the 56 to be prosecuted, party officials said.

The upheaval in Gujral's Janata Dal party came at a particularly sensitive time as the government intended to present the pathbreaking 1997/98 (April-March) budget to parliament during a session starting on Wednesday.
"The imminent prosecution of Laloo Prasad Yadav in the fodder scam threatens to plunge the fledgling Gujral government into its first major crisis," the Indian Express said.

"Mr Yadav's refusal to step down will create dissension within the Front and further erode its fragile cohesion and commitment to transparency, accountability and the rule of law," the Economic Times said.
